rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited unless strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives in Article 5(1), point (h). First, the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)). Second, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)). Third, the localisation or identification of a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences listed in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Use is confined to confirming a specifically targeted individual's identity and requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27) and EU-database registration (Article 49), which for law-enforcement systems occurs in a secure non-public section holding only the Annex VIII Section A, B and C and Annex IX points specified in Article 49(4)(a) to (d), accessible solely to the Commission and Article 74(8) authorities.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons as a permitted objective.
The answer clearly identifies the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine terrorist threat, as a permitted objective.
The answer correctly specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for serious offences listed in Annex II punishable by at least four years’ imprisonment as a permitted objective.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear, complete sentences without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Article 50(2) governs. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, so far as technically feasible, having regard to the specificities and limitations of various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer explicitly says outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer includes that solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer refers to feasibility being assessed with regard to content specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input/semantics, and law enforcement authorization.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, complete sentences and logical structure.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). Those powers are exercised taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union based on the Treaties (Article 88(1)). National market surveillance authorities hold no enforcement competence over Chapter V; without prejudice to Article 75(3), they may only request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where that is necessary and proportionate to assist with the fulfilment of their own tasks under the Regulation (Article 88(2)). Consistently with that allocation, providers of general-purpose AI models must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities (Article 53(3)), keep Annex XI technical documentation for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities (Article 53(1)(a)), and systemic-risk providers must report serious incidents without undue delay to the AI Office (Article 55(1)(c)).
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V.
The candidate answer clearly states that the Commission entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing a high-risk AI system in real world conditions may be transferred to a third country only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). This is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met for the testing itself to be lawful, so the transfer condition operates in addition to, and not in substitution for, the other conditions in that paragraph, including that the subjects have given informed consent under Article 60(4)(i), which carries the right of withdrawal and immediate, permanent deletion of their personal data under Article 60(5). Article 60 sets no further, transfer-specific requirement; the safeguards standard is by reference to Union law generally. The items listed in the answer shape as Article 10(5)(a), (f) have no supporting text in the supplied evidence and are not addressed.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by explicitly requiring that 'appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented' for data transfers, which directly reflects the requirement in Article 60(4)(e).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, third-person regulatory style without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions: (a) it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; or (b) based on a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Either limb alone suffices. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption, not a third condition: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under point (a) when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. Under Article 51(3) the Commission may amend those thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act to reflect the state of the art.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, as specified in Article 51(2).

The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, either ex officio or following a qualified alert, based on equivalence to high-impact capabilities using Annex XIII criteria, is sufficient for classification.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives and not cumulative, and confirms that either limb alone suffices.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a clear, actionable manner consistent with regulatory guidance.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Classification under the Annex I route requires both conditions in Article 6(1) to be fulfilled cumulatively. Article 6(1)(a) is satisfied: the system is a safety component of a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed at Annex I, point 11. But Article 6(1)(b) requires that the product be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, and a Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so that condition fails. It would be high-risk only if it separately falls within an Annex III use case under Article 6(2).
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the conclusion, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions in Article 6(1) must be fulfilled cumulatively.
The answer correctly explains that MDR Class I devices of this type are self-certified without notified body involvement, i.e., no third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that condition (b) fails and therefore Article 6(1) does not apply, directly stating the logical consequence.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear logical structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift qualifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1), provided both cumulative conditions are met. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift or the safety component itself must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable here, as it concerns only AI systems listed in Annex III. Conformity assessment follows Article 43(3): the procedure required by Directive 2014/33/EU applies, with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as its unambiguous position, matching the criterion.

The answer specifies that the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and identifies Directive 2014/33/EU for lifts as falling under Annex I, point 4.

The answer states that the product (the lift or the safety component) must be subject to third-party conformity assessment under the relevant Directive, which reflects the substance of Article 6(1)(b).
The answer explicitly refers to 'both cumulative conditions' and structures the explanation around their joint fulfillment, making clear that both are required.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured, coherent prose with logical flow suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, professional, and uses the precise regulatory language without any self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both, the two duties are cumulative and both immediate, and neither is deferred pending the authority's involvement. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the Article 44 certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The authority's evaluation under Article 79(2) is additional, not a substitute: it may require corrective action within a prescribed period, the operator must extend that action to all systems concerned (Article 79(4)), and inadequate action triggers provisional measures under Article 79(5).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties are cumulative and immediate.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's duty to immediately take corrective action upon awareness of non-compliance.
The answer clearly assigns the duty to investigate causes to the provider under Article 20(2), stating it must be done immediately.
The answer specifies that investigation is done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and does not defer to the market surveillance authority.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with proper legal references and logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate: Article 24(3) states in terms that distributors shall ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2. The "where applicable" qualifier answers the operator's objection, the duty bites where there is something physical or logistical to safeguard, such as a system embedded in or shipped with a product, supplied on hardware or media, or transferred with its accompanying CE marking, EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use. If conditions do compromise conformity, Article 24(2) bars you from making the system available until it is brought into conformity, and Article 24(4) requires corrective action, withdrawal or recall once it is on the market.
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the local model's statement.
The answer directly cites and applies Article 24(3) to the scenario, stating its relevance to distributors.

The answer explains that the duty applies 'where applicable' and clarifies this qualifier by referencing physical or logistical elements like embedded systems, hardware, media, or accompanying documentation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained explanation without self-reference or hedging; structured in clear, coherent prose suitable for regulatory guidance.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: Drones are neither prohibited nor high-risk as such, neither Article 5 nor Annex III names them; the AI's purpose decides. Using a drone to identify who is around town is real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces: prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) where the purpose is law enforcement, save three exhaustive derogations, targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons; prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or of a terrorist attack; localisation or identification of a suspect of a listed offence punishable by at least four years, each requiring prior authorisation under Article 5(3). Inferring race, political opinions, union membership, beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation from that footage is separately prohibited by Article 5(1)(g). Outside the law-enforcement prohibition, remote biometric identification is high-risk under Annex III.1(a). A toy drone is high-risk only through Article 6(1): the AI must be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I.2) and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, otherwise it is not high-risk, though Article 5's prohibitions still bind. Toy drones in other applications run the same two-limb Article 6(1) test, failing which Annex III's listed uses apply; Article 50(1) transparency attaches if the system interacts directly with natural persons.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that drones are not inherently high-risk or prohibited, and that classification depends on the AI system's intended use under Article 6.

Correctly identifies that using AI in a drone to identify people in public constitutes remote biometric identification, which is either prohibited (in law enforcement contexts) or classified as high-risk under Annex III.1(a), and clarifies it does not fall under the 1:1 verification exclusion.
Explains that the toy status of the drone is irrelevant and that classification depends on intended use, not the device type.
States that a toy drone used for other applications is assessed under the same Article 6(1) criteria or Annex III, meaning high-risk status depends on whether the use matches those provisions.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise regulatory reasoning; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. As deployer the operator is bound to use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use (Article 26), so a use outside the stated intended purpose is already non-compliant; and if you modify the intended purpose of a high-risk system already on the market the operator becomes its provider with all provider obligations (Article 25(1)). The operator's counsel's "no risk" view is not decisive: the Annex I product route (safety component of, or a product covered by, the listed legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment) and the Annex III listed-use route are separate tests, and even an Annex III system escapes only through the documented Article 6(3) derogation, never through profiling of natural persons. Annex I covers machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, in-vitro diagnostics, civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry tractors, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle approval, vehicle general safety, and civil aviation. Logs automatically generated must be retained for at least six months (Article 26(6)). The evidence supplied contains no text for Articles 10(2), 12(2) or 43(1).(1), 12(2) or 43(1), so those provisions are not assessed here.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply proceed,' which matches the required 'No' verdict for criterion 1.
The answer explains that use must be in accordance with the instructions for use under Article 26 and that deviation is non-compliant, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The answer affirms that logs must be retained for at least six months under Article 26(6), satisfying the logging requirement regardless of the specific use.
rows.tone_remark: Inappropriate due to self-referential statement about 'the evidence supplied contains no text...', which introduces meta-commentary about the input materials, violating professional regulatory tone.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. Clinical decision-support software recommending best treatment is potentially high-risk, and the governing route is Article 6(1) read with Annex I, point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices), not Annex III. Article 6(1)(a) is met where the AI system is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation; Article 6(1)(b) requires that product to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, satisfied where the software is a notified-body-assessed medical device class. The Article 6(3) derogation for narrow procedural, confirmatory or preparatory tasks is unavailable, as it applies only to Annex III systems. Separately, Annex III, point 5(d) captures emergency healthcare patient triage systems, a distinct use case from treatment recommendation.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' and affirms the system is potentially high-risk, matching the required verdict.
The answer cites Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and explains why 6(1) applies, thus not stating the substance of criterion 2.
The answer explicitly states the system is not covered by Annex III, arguing instead for classification under Annex I, thus contradicting the required substance of criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured explanation using precise regulatory language without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Annex XII (applied through Article 53(1)(b)) governs: yes to the first four, no to the last. Date of release and methods of distribution must be disclosed, Annex XII.1(c). Number of parameters must be disclosed, together with the architecture, Annex XII.1(f). How the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself must be disclosed where applicable, Annex XII.1(d). The licence for the model must be disclosed, Annex XII.1(h). Samples of outlier training data need not be: Annex XII.2(c) requires only the type and provenance of training, testing and validation data and the curation methodologies, not data samples. Disclosure is without prejudice to intellectual property and trade secrets, and Article 53(2) disapplies Article 53(1)(b) for free and open-source models unless they carry systemic risk.
criteria_text: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the date of release must be disclosed, citing Annex XII.1(c).
The answer clearly states that the number of parameters must be disclosed, along with architecture, under Annex XII.1(f).
The answer confirms disclosure of interaction with hardware or software under Annex XII.1(d), specifying applicability conditions.
The answer affirms that the license must be disclosed, referencing Annex XII.1(h).
The answer correctly states that samples of outlier training data need not be disclosed, explaining that only type, provenance, and curation methods are required under Annex XII.2(c).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(2), an Annex III system is high-risk only where it falls within a listed use-case under one of the eight areas, which are: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). No, healthcare decision-making is not itself one of those areas. Health appears only as specific use-cases inside Annex III.5: evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them (Annex III.5(a)); risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)); and triage of emergency calls and emergency healthcare patient triage (Annex III.5(d)). Clinical AI otherwise reaches high-risk status through the Annex I product route under Article 6(1), for example as a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device requiring third-party conformity assessment (Annex I.11, .12).
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The answer lists all eight areas of high-risk use cases as specified in Annex III, using equivalent wording and clear references.
The answer explicitly states 'No, healthcare decision-making is not itself one of those areas,' which matches the required verdict.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails alone cannot move an agentic system out of the high-risk class. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on whether the system falls within a listed Annex III use-case, judged by its intended purpose, not on the strength of its mitigations; Article 8(1) confirms that requirements apply "taking into account their intended purpose," with the Article 9 risk-management system serving compliance, not reclassification. Guardrails are precisely the Article 9(2)(d) mitigation and control measures, and their residual-risk effect is reported, not credited against classification. They must instead be documented: in the Annex IV technical documentation (system description, design specifications and architecture, and the risk-management measures) and in the Article 13(3)(b) instructions for use, intended purpose (i), tested accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (ii), foreseeable circumstances including reasonably foreseeable misuse creating risk (iii), output-explanation capabilities (iv), performance on specific persons or groups (v), input-data specifications (vi), and information enabling correct interpretation of output (vii), with Article 12(2) logging covering start/stop, input reference data and post-market-monitoring-relevant events. Changing capabilities and intended use can change the outcome, but only by genuinely removing the system from the Annex III use-case or by satisfying an Article 6(3) condition (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting patterns without influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task) with no significant risk, never where the system profiles natural persons, supported by a documented pre-market self-assessment. Conversely, modifying intended purpose so a non-high-risk system becomes high-risk, or substantially modifying one that remains high-risk, makes the modifier a provider under Article 25(1)(b), (c).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer states that guardrails alone cannot move a system out of high-risk classification and correctly explains that the derogation in Article 6(3) is binary, not creating intermediate risk tiers.
The answer identifies the four Article 6(3) conditions by substance, listing them explicitly and linking exemption to meeting one of these intended-use conditions.
The answer confirms that changing capabilities and intended use can change risk classification if the new purpose satisfies an Article 6(3) condition, which matches the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that profiling systems are always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or changes, directly reflecting the exception in Article 6(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; information is logically ordered and actionable.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted, it is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), but the artificial nature must be disclosed. Where the images resemble existing persons or clinical situations and would falsely appear authentic, they are a deep fake within Article 3(60), so the university as deployer must disclose under Article 50(4) that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The lighter regime does not apply: the law-enforcement exemption in Article 50(4) covers only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and the attenuated "appropriate manner" disclosure is confined to evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, educational illustration is not such a work. The provider must separately ensure machine-readable marking under Article 50(2).
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted and not prohibited under Article 5(1), which affirms permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep fakes, including when used in educational contexts resembling authentic clinical situations.

The answer states the lighter regime does not apply because educational illustration is not an artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, contradicting the criterion that the lighter regime does apply as an analogous work.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption limited to specific criminal purposes and confirms it does not apply here.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the tool is neither prohibited nor high-risk. Annex III, point 6 covers AI systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities for offence-related risk assessment or profiling; a retailer running its own loss-prevention checks is not such an authority acting for law-enforcement purposes, so the listed use-case is not met and Article 6(2) is not triggered. Article 5(1)(d) is likewise not engaged: the flag rests on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a possible offence, current-cart and checkout anomalies, not solely on profiling or personality traits, and it only supports the staff member's human assessment. Article 5(1)(c) fails too: no evaluation over a certain period of time yielding a social score, no detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts (point (i)) and none disproportionate to the behaviour (point (ii)), the bag check being optional and contemporaneous.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Annex III, point 6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and that the retailer does not fall within that category.
The answer explains that a retailer running its own loss-prevention checks is not acting as or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, thus falling outside the scope of Annex III.6.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents a logical flow suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2. Those are substantive requirements attaching to the high-risk AI system itself, and Article 43(3) states expressly that they "shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment". Article 43(3) also governs the operator's exact scenario: where a legal act listed in Section A of Annex I lets the product manufacturer opt out of third-party conformity assessment on the basis of having applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, that manufacturer may use the option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out is therefore conditional on Section 2 compliance, not an exemption from it; if any Section 2 requirement is uncovered by a harmonised standard or common specification, the option is unavailable. Nor does opting out remove high-risk status under Article 6(1), Article 43(3) presupposes the system remains high-risk. Article 43(1)(a), (d) does not apply to the operator: it governs the Annex VI internal-control route for Annex III point 1 systems. The supplied evidence contains no text for Article 41(1)(a)'s sub-points.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2', which matches the required verdict of 'No'.
The answer quotes and explains that Section 2 requirements 'shall apply' and 'shall be part of that assessment', conveying the substance that they remain integral to the conformity process.

The answer explains that the opt-out is conditional on having applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering *all* Section 2 requirements, directly addressing the criterion's substance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically ordered and actionable.
